text: ☰ ☀ The Ether Gazette Archive & Search Browse the Archive A Weekly Dispatch for the Student Registered Nurse Anesthetist The Ether Gazette “Vigilance, distilled.” Week of July 6, 2026 Vol. 1, No. 2 Est. 2026 📰 Headlines Two Class I Anesthesia Workstation Recalls Put Ventilator Power Failures in the Spotlight The FDA's most serious recall category now covers two mainstream anesthesia machine lines at once. GE HealthCare's Carestation 600/700 series can shut down unexpectedly and reboot to factory defaults if AC mains power is lost and restored — silently dropping ventilation settings mid-case. Separately, Dräger expanded a correction for its Atlan A350/A350XL workstations after a manufacturing defect in the piston ventilator was found capable of causing ventilation failure, sometimes flagged only by a terse "Ventilator error!!!" message. Neither manufacturer has reported patient injury, but both now instruct clinicians to keep a self-inflating bag at hand and to treat any power event or ventilator alarm as a cue to switch to manual ventilation immediately. FDA · GE HealthCare CareStation Anesthesia Systems Correction & Dräger Atlan A350/A350XL Correction CMS's 2026 Fee Schedule Nets Anesthesiologists a Bare 0.88 Percent Bump The finalized CY 2026 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule sets the anesthesia conversion factor at $20.4976 — up just 0.88 percent from 2025, and $20.5998 for clinicians in Advanced Alternative Payment Models. ASA notes that a 2.5 percent statutory increase from last year's budget bill was largely offset by a new -2.5 percent "efficiency adjustment" CMS applied to non-time-based services, plus a roughly 7 percent cut to facility-based payments (partly offset by a 4 percent bump for non-facility settings). Advocacy groups call the net effect a real-terms pay cut once inflation is factored in. ASA · CMS Finalizes Policies Undermining Anesthesia Payments Cal State Fullerton's Nurse Anesthesia Program Climbs to No. 3 Nationally U.S. News & World Report's 2026 Best Graduate Schools rankings move Cal State Fullerton's nurse anesthesia program — run jointly with Kaiser Permanente's School of Anesthesia — from No. 7 to No. 3 in the country, and No. 1 in California, tying UNC Chapel Hill. Program leadership credits the depth of the Kaiser Permanente clinical partnership for the jump, a reminder of how much a strong clinical-site relationship can shape a program's trajectory. CSUF News · US News & World Report Ranks Nursing Anesthesia Program No. 3 in Nation AANA Foundation Awards $278,250 in Scholarships to Nurse Anesthesia Students The AANA Foundation reports it fielded 386 competitive scholarship applications in FY25 and funded 94 of them, for a combined $278,250 — a reminder, as SRNAs head into another tuition cycle, that the Foundation's application windows are worth calendaring alongside clinical rotations. AANA · AANA Foundation Resident Scholarships 🎓 Upcoming Webinars Methadone and Dexmedetomidine in the Perioperative Period: Global Practices and Controversies Free CE IARS · Tuesday, July 14, 2026 · 4:30–6:00 PM ET · Live interactive webinar An international panel compares how clinicians in different countries use methadone and dexmedetomidine perioperatively, working through real-world practice patterns and where the evidence does — and doesn't — support current habits. Register at aana.com → 📚 From the Literature New Guidance Simplifies Genetic Testing for Malignant Hyperthermia Risk A special article proposes a practical, three-question screen clinicians can use before deciding whether a patient needs formal malignant hyperthermia (MH) genetic workup: has the patient had an MH reaction or known susceptibility; does a family member have MH susceptibility or a reaction history; and has the patient or a relative already been genetically tested, with what result. Sequencing of RYR1 , CACNA1S , and STAC3 remains the backbone of confirmatory testing, but the authors are candid that a negative panel does not fully clear a patient — "no patient can ever be at zero risk" — so relatives of confirmed cases and patients with high-risk variants should still be managed as MH-susceptible even without a personal reaction history. Riazi, S., Watt, S., Plester, J., & Biesecker, L. G. (2026). A proposed North American approach for genetic testing of individuals at risk for malignant hyperthermia. Anesthesiology, 144 (4), 776–783. https://doi.org/10.1097/ALN.0000000000005849 ⚖️ Legislation & Scope Tracker Following up on last week's watch list. Florida's HB 375 Dies in the Senate — Autonomous CRNA Practice Waits Another Year The bill we flagged last week as "eyeing a July 1 effective date" didn't make it. HB 375 passed the Florida House 78–28 on February 4, but its Senate companion, SB 462, died in the Health Policy Committee, and HB 375 itself died in the Senate Rules Committee on March 13 without a floor vote. The measure would have let qualified CRNAs register as autonomous advanced practice registered nurses and practice without physician oversight; supporters are expected to refile next session, following the same path as predecessor bills HB 649 (died 2025) and HB 257 (died 2024). Florida Senate · HB 375 (2026) Bill History The National Count Holds at 37 Opt-Out States Plus D.C. With Florida's push stalled for another cycle, the national scope-of-practice map is effectively unchanged this week: 37 states plus the District of Columbia have opted out of the federal Medicare physician-supervision requirement, though roughly 29 states plus D.C. pair that opt-out with true full, independent state-law practice authority. The gap between the two — a federal billing waiver versus an actual state-law grant of independence — is exactly the terrain bills like HB 375 keep trying, and failing, to close. Always confirm against the live ASHP and FDA shortage databases before making clinical decisions — status changes daily and this table could not be cross-checked against the live ASHP database this week. 💡 Knowledge Pearl Dantrolene works upstream of the calcium overload that drives malignant hyperthermia. MH is triggered by volatile anesthetics or succinylcholine in genetically susceptible patients (most often via RYR1 mutations), causing the ryanodine receptor on the sarcoplasmic reticulum to dump calcium into the muscle cytoplasm uncontrollably. That flood of calcium drives sustained contraction, runaway heat production, and skyrocketing oxygen consumption — the hypermetabolic state that produces the classic triad of rising end-tidal CO2, muscle rigidity, and fever. Dantrolene binds the RYR1 receptor directly and blocks calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, cutting off the process at its source rather than just treating the downstream fever or acidosis. Initial dosing is 2.5 mg/kg IV, repeated every 5–10 minutes until symptoms resolve — there is no fixed maximum in an ongoing crisis. Because a single reaction doesn't fully rule a patient out or in, current guidance leans on a short screening history (personal or family MH reaction, and any prior genetic testing) to decide who actually needs formal RYR1 / CACNA1S / STAC3 sequencing, rather than testing everyone with a vague family rumor of "anesthesia problems." 🕰️ This Week in Anesthesia History June 17, 1931 On June 17, 1931, Agatha Hodgins founded the National Association of Nurse Anesthetists — the organization that would become today's AANA — in Cleveland, Ohio. Hodgins, who had already helped establish nurse anesthesia training at Lakeside Hospital and co-founded the Lakeside Alumnae Association of Nurse Anesthetists a decade earlier, built the national association specifically to defend nurse anesthetists' right to practice against a wave of early-20th-century legal challenges arguing that administering anesthesia constituted the unlicensed practice of medicine. Nearly a century later, the fight over who gets to define and defend that scope of practice — see this week's Legislation Tracker — is still very much alive. 🧠 Board Question of the Week Per the ASA's 2026 practice guideline, a patient undergoing an open abdominal procedure receives a bilateral transversus abdominis plane (TAP) block as part of a multimodal analgesia plan. Which of the following best describes what this fascial plane block actually accomplishes? A It blocks visceral afferents from the abdominal organs, eliminating deep intra-abdominal pain B It blocks somatic sensory afferents (roughly T6–L1) supplying the anterior abdominal wall, reducing incisional pain and opioid need C It blocks sympathetic chain fibers, producing a spinal-like sympathectomy and blood pressure drop D It blocks phrenic nerve fibers, reducing diaphragmatic irritation from pneumoperitoneum Correct answer: B — Somatic sensory afferents of the anterior abdominal wall A TAP block deposits local anesthetic in the fascial plane between the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles, where the somatic sensory nerves supplying the anterior abdominal wall (roughly T6–L1) travel. It reliably reduces incisional (somatic) pain and opioid consumption in the first 24 postoperative hours — exactly the outcome the 2026 ASA guideline's "strong" recommendation is based on — but it does not touch visceral pain from the bowel, peritoneum, or other organs, which travels via separate autonomic pathways. A is wrong because visceral afferents aren't in the TAP plane at all, which is why patients still need systemic multimodal analgesia for deep visceral discomfort. C describes neuraxial (spinal/epidural) sympathetic blockade, not a peripheral fascial plane block. D is incorrect — the phrenic nerve runs nowhere near the TAP plane; diaphragmatic irritation from pneumoperitoneum isn't addressed by this block. ☰ ☀ A Weekly Dispatch for the Student Registered Nurse Anesthetist The Ether Gazette “Vigilance, distilled.” Week of July 1, 2026 Vol. 1, No. 1 Est. 2026 📰 Headlines A New Protocol Cuts Unnecessary Eye Consults After Surgery The Anesthesia Patient Safety Foundation has published a practical, anesthesiology-led protocol for managing postoperative corneal abrasions — the most common ocular injury of the perioperative period, typically caused by incomplete eyelid closure (lagophthalmos) under general anesthesia. Early data show the stepwise approach resolves symptoms without routine ophthalmology referral, sparing patients cost and delay while keeping serious injuries from being missed. APSF · Managing Postoperative Corneal Abrasions: A Protocol for Anesthesiology Teams CRNA Ranks Projected to Grow 10 Percent by 2033 New workforce figures put the current U.S. CRNA population at roughly 67,700 — about 200 per 100,000 people — with federal projections calling for 10 percent growth through 2033, or about 5,200 new positions. The report frames the growth against persistent rural anesthesia-access gaps and an aging surgical population driving case volume upward. Becker's ASC · The CRNA Workforce in 2026: 10 Things to Know FDA Clears Single-Dose Propofol Vials as Manufacturers Chase a Chronic Shortage Amneal Pharmaceuticals has won FDA approval for a single-dose propofol injectable emulsion, with production on a dedicated in-house line intended to insulate supply from the raw-material and contract-manufacturing disruptions that have kept propofol on shortage lists for years. It's a meaningful step, but as this week's Drug Shortage Watch below shows, propofol is not out of the woods yet. Pharmacy Times · Propofol Injectable Emulsion Single-Dose Vials Receive FDA Approval California's AB 876 Takes Effect, Formalizing CRNA Anesthesia Authority As of January 1, 2026, AB 876 defines "anesthesia services" in California law and confirms that a patient-specific anesthesia order fully authorizes a CRNA's care, clarifying that medication selection under that order is not a "prescription." The law codifies long-standing practice rather than expanding it — CRNAs remain subject to existing supervision, credentialing, and facility bylaw requirements — but supporters say it closes ambiguity that had been used to challenge CRNA billing and hospital privileging. Register at northwestseminars.com → 📚 From the Literature ASA's New Pain Guideline Makes Fascial Plane Blocks the Default, Not the Exception The ASA Task Force on Perioperative Pain Management now strongly recommends fascial plane blocks (e.g., erector spinae plane, transversus abdominis plane, PECS) to cut pain and opioid use in the first 24 postoperative hours for open cardiothoracic, abdominal, retroperitoneal, and pelvic surgery, plus mastectomy — with a conditional nod for minimally invasive cases and open hernia repair. Pediatric recommendations follow the same logic for open cardiac and thoracic surgery. The Task Force is candid about the ceiling on this evidence: many underlying trials are small, single-center, and inconsistently designed, so the "strong" label reflects a strong opioid-sparing signal more than definitive outcome data. Joshi, G. P., Mariano, E. R., Elkassabany, N. M., et al. (American Society of Anesthesiologists Task Force on Perioperative Pain Management). (2026). 2026 American Society of Anesthesiologists practice guideline on perioperative pain management using local and regional analgesia for cardiothoracic surgeries, mastectomy, and abdominal surgeries. Anesthesiology, 144 (1), 19–43. https://doi.org/10.1097/ALN.0000000000005790 ⚖️ Legislation & Scope Tracker Where independent CRNA practice stands as of this week. Florida's HB 375 Clears Committee, Eyes a July 1 Effective Date HB 375 would let CRNAs register as autonomous advanced practice registered nurses under Florida's existing APRN statute and practice without physician oversight — though individual hospitals could still impose their own protocol requirements. The bill has passed both the Health Professions & Programs and Health & Human Services committees; a companion bill, SB 462, is moving in the Senate. As drafted, HB 375 would take effect July 1, 2026, if signed — worth watching closely this week. Florida Senate · HB 375 (2026) Bill History The National Picture: Opt-Out Is Not the Same as Full Practice Authority As of this year, 37 states plus D.C. have opted out of the federal Medicare physician-supervision requirement for CRNAs — but opt-out is a CMS billing waiver, not a scope-of-practice grant. Only 23 states plus D.C. currently give CRNAs true full, independent practice authority under state nurse practice acts; the rest still layer on collaborative-agreement or setting-based restrictions even after opting out. That gap between federal waiver and state law is exactly what bills like Florida's HB 375 and California's AB 876 are trying to close. Always confirm against the live ASHP and FDA shortage databases before making clinical decisions — status changes daily. 💡 Knowledge Pearl Sugammadex reverses rocuronium and vecuronium by encapsulation, not enzyme inhibition. Unlike neostigmine, which reverses neuromuscular blockade indirectly by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase and raising synaptic acetylcholine, sugammadex is a modified gamma-cyclodextrin that forms a tight 1:1 host-guest complex directly around the steroidal neuromuscular blocker molecule in the plasma. This encapsulation creates a concentration gradient that pulls free rocuronium or vecuronium off nicotinic receptors and out of the neuromuscular junction, back into plasma for renal clearance as an inactive complex. The practical payoff: sugammadex can reverse even profound (deep) blockade reliably, works faster than neostigmine at comparable depths, and — because it doesn't act on acetylcholinesterase — carries none of neostigmine's muscarinic side effects (bradycardia, bronchospasm, secretions), so it doesn't require co-administration with an antimuscarinic like glycopyrrolate. It has no reversal activity against benzylisoquinolinium blockers (e.g., cisatracurium) or succinylcholine, since those aren't steroidal molecules it can encapsulate. 🕰️ This Week in Anesthesia History July 1940 In July 1940, the American Society of Anesthesiologists published the first issue of Anesthesiology , under founding editor-in-chief Henry S. Ruth, MD. It was a deliberate act of professionalization: anesthesia had only recently begun separating from surgery as its own discipline, and a dedicated, peer-reviewed journal gave the young specialty a place to build a real evidence base rather than passing technique down purely by apprenticeship. Eight and a half decades later, Anesthesiology remains the field's flagship journal — including, this month, the very 2026 practice guideline covered above. 🧠 Board Question of the Week A patient receiving a ropivacaine infusion for a continuous interscalene nerve block develops perioral numbness, tinnitus, and then a witnessed tonic-clonic seizure 20 minutes after catheter bolus dosing. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management, assuming the airway is secured and seizure activity is controlled? A Administer high-dose epinephrine (1 mg IV) per standard ACLS arrest dosing B Give a second local anesthetic bolus through the catheter to "burn off" the receptor C Begin 20% lipid emulsion therapy (bolus followed by continuous infusion) D Administer flumazenil to reverse the neurologic toxicity Correct answer: C — Begin 20% lipid emulsion therapy This presentation is classic local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST): early CNS signs (perioral numbness, tinnitus, metallic taste) progressing to seizure, which can precede cardiovascular collapse. Per ASRA's LAST checklist, once the airway/seizure is managed, first-line treatment is 20% lipid emulsion — typically a 1.5 mL/kg bolus over 2–3 minutes followed by a 0.25 mL/kg/min infusion — which acts as a "lipid sink," partitioning lipophilic local anesthetic away from cardiac and neural tissue. A is wrong because ACLS-dose epinephrine (versus the reduced <1 mcg/kg boluses ASRA recommends in LAST) can worsen arrhythmias and impair lipid resuscitation. B is wrong and dangerous — more local anesthetic deepens toxicity. D treats benzodiazepine toxicity, not LAST, and doesn't address the underlying problem.
